q: A 34-year-old woman presents with 3 months of fatigue and pica (craving ice). She is a vegetarian with menorrhagia. Examination shows conjunctival pallor and koilonychia. Full blood count: Hb 92 g/L, MCV 71 fL, MCH 24 pg, platelets 465 ×10^9/L, WCC 6.1 ×10^9/L. The blood film shows hypochromic microcytic red cells with pencil cells and anisopoikilocytosis. Ferritin is 6 µg/L (15–300), serum iron low, total iron-binding capacity raised and transferrin saturation 8%. She is otherwise well with no gastrointestinal symptoms. Which single investigation finding, if present, would be MOST consistent with the underlying diagnosis?
explain: This is classic iron-deficiency anaemia (IDA): microcytic hypochromic indices, low ferritin, high TIBC, low transferrin saturation, pencil cells and reactive thrombocytosis. 🩸 In iron deficiency, depleted iron stores upregulate the soluble (serum) transferrin receptor (sTfR), so it rises. sTfR is especially useful to distinguish IDA from anaemia of chronic disease, where ferritin may be normal/high but sTfR remains normal. Ferritin is the single most useful test (low = diagnostic per BSH), but it is an acute-phase reactant. TIBC/transferrin is raised (not low) and transferrin saturation is low in IDA. RDW is characteristically raised (anisocytosis), not reduced. BSH guidance mandates investigating the cause; in this woman menorrhagia plus vegetarianism explains it, but GI loss must be excluded if unexplained.

Ferritin is the single most useful test (low = diagnostic per BSH), but it is an acute-phase reactant. TIBC/transferrin is raised (not low) and transferrin saturation is low in IDA. RDW is characteristically raised (anisocytosis), not reduced. A.html: Ferritin is low (6 µg/L) in iron deficiency, reflecting depleted stores. A raised ferritin would point to iron overload, inflammation or anaemia of chronic disease rather than IDA, and is inconsistent with the low transferrin saturation given here.

B.html: TIBC is raised in iron deficiency because low iron stores upregulate transferrin synthesis. A low TIBC is typical of anaemia of chronic disease, not IDA, and would not fit this transferrin saturation of 8%.

C.html: Correct. Iron depletion upregulates cellular transferrin receptors, so soluble transferrin receptor rises. It is normal in anaemia of chronic disease, making it the discriminating marker of true tissue iron deficiency here.

D.html: RDW is characteristically increased in iron deficiency due to marked anisocytosis (variation in red cell size). A reduced RDW would be unusual and points away from evolving iron deficiency.

E.html: Transferrin saturation is low (8% here) in iron deficiency. A raised saturation suggests iron overload such as haemochromatosis, which is incompatible with the low ferritin and microcytosis described.

q: A 68-year-old man presents with 6 months of progressive numbness in both feet, unsteadiness and fatigue. He follows a strict vegan diet and takes omeprazole for reflux. Examination reveals a lemon-yellow tinge to the skin, glossitis, absent ankle reflexes, extensor plantars and impaired proprioception. Full blood count: Hb 84 g/L, MCV 116 fL, WCC 3.2 ×10^9/L, platelets 118 ×10^9/L. Blood film shows oval macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Bilirubin is mildly raised and lactate dehydrogenase markedly elevated. Which single mechanism BEST explains his neurological signs?
options: Impaired myelin synthesis from defective methylation
Accumulation of phytanic acid in Schwann cells
Ischaemic infarction of the dorsal columns
explain: This is vitamin B12 deficiency with subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD): dorsal column loss (proprioception, unsteadiness), corticospinal signs (extensor plantars) plus peripheral neuropathy (absent ankle reflexes). Veganism and long-term PPI use both impair B12 status. The macrocytic anaemia, pancytopenia, hypersegmented neutrophils, raised LDH and bilirubin reflect ineffective erythropoiesis. 🧠 Mechanism: B12 is a cofactor for methionine synthase, which converts homocysteine to methionine, regenerating tetrahydrofolate and producing S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). SAM is the universal methyl donor for myelin basic protein and phospholipid methylation. Deficient methylation disrupts myelin maintenance, producing the demyelination of the dorsal and lateral columns. Management (BSH): treat with intramuscular hydroxocobalamin; if both B12 and folate are low, replace B12 first to avoid precipitating/worsening SACD. Neurological cases receive alternate-day IM B12 until no further improvement.

B.html: Autoimmune peripheral demyelination describes chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy, not B12 deficiency. It would not produce macrocytic anaemia, hypersegmented neutrophils or the combined dorsal-column and corticospinal picture seen here.

C.html: Phytanic acid accumulation causes Refsum disease, a rare peroxisomal disorder with retinitis pigmentosa and cerebellar signs. It is unrelated to megaloblastic anaemia and does not explain this clinical and haematological picture.

D.html: Copper deficiency can mimic SACD with myelopathy, but it does not cause megaloblastic change with hypersegmented neutrophils and oval macrocytes. The vegan diet, PPI use and classic film point squarely to B12 deficiency.

q: A 22-year-old man of Nigerian heritage is admitted with severe generalised bone pain 2 days after starting co-trimoxazole for a chest infection. He is known to have a haemoglobinopathy. Observations: temperature 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 94% on air. Full blood count: Hb 68 g/L (baseline 82 g/L), reticulocytes 12%, WCC 14 ×10^9/L. Blood film shows sickled cells, target cells and Howell–Jolly bodies. He is in severe pain scoring 9/10 despite paracetamol taken at home. There are no chest signs and chest radiograph is clear. Which single intervention is the MOST important immediate priority?
options: Prompt strong opioid analgesia within 30 minutes
Immediate top-up red cell transfusion to baseline
explain: This is an acute sickle cell vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis, precipitated by infection. Howell–Jolly bodies confirm functional hyposplenism. NICE (CG143) and BSH guidance are explicit: an acute painful crisis is a medical emergency and strong analgesia (a bolus of opioid such as morphine) must be offered within 30 minutes of arrival, with pain reassessed every 30 minutes. 💉 Mechanism: deoxygenated HbS polymerises, deforming red cells into rigid sickled shapes that occlude the microvasculature, causing ischaemic bone pain. Rapid, adequate analgesia is the single highest immediate priority. Avoid routine transfusion for uncomplicated painful crisis — top-up transfusion is not indicated unless there is severe anaemia below baseline with symptoms or aplastic/sequestration crisis; exchange transfusion is reserved for acute chest syndrome, stroke or multi-organ failure. Antibiotics, oxygen, hydration and thromboprophylaxis are important, but immediate analgesia comes first.

B.html: Correct. NICE CG143 mandates offering strong opioid analgesia within 30 minutes of presentation in an acute painful sickle crisis, with frequent reassessment. Rapid effective analgesia is the single most important immediate step for this severe pain.

C.html: Antibiotics are appropriate given the precipitating chest infection and hyposplenism, but the immediate, time-critical priority in an acute painful crisis is analgesia within 30 minutes. Antibiotics and sepsis screening follow promptly but do not take precedence over pain control.

q: A 62-year-old man is referred with pruritus that is worse after hot baths, facial plethora and headaches. He has had a deep vein thrombosis. Examination shows splenomegaly. Full blood count: Hb 191 g/L, haematocrit 0.58, WCC 13.5 ×10^9/L, platelets 520 ×10^9/L. Serum erythropoietin is low. Arterial oxygen saturation is 97%. A mutation analysis is requested. Which single result would MOST strongly confirm the diagnosis?
explain: This is polycythaemia vera (PV): raised haematocrit, aquagenic pruritus (itch after hot baths), plethora, splenomegaly, thrombosis and a suppressed erythropoietin indicating a primary (rather than secondary/hypoxic) erythrocytosis. 🩸 Mechanism: the JAK2 V617F point mutation causes constitutive activation of JAK2 tyrosine kinase, producing erythropoietin-independent proliferation of the erythroid (and other myeloid) lineages. It is present in over 95% of PV cases; the remainder carry JAK2 exon 12 mutations. WHO/BSH diagnostic criteria combine raised Hb/haematocrit, the JAK2 mutation and (if needed) a hypercellular trephine with low EPO. CALR and MPL mutations occur in essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis but essentially never in PV. BCR-ABL1 defines CML. FLT3-ITD is an AML prognostic marker. Management of PV includes venesection to keep haematocrit below 0.45, aspirin, and cytoreduction (hydroxycarbamide) in high-risk patients.

It is present in over 95% of PV cases; the remainder carry JAK2 exon 12 mutations. CALR and MPL mutations occur in essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis but essentially never in PV. BCR-ABL1 defines CML. FLT3-ITD is an AML prognostic marker. Management of PV includes venesection to keep haematocrit below 0.45, aspirin, and cytoreduction (hydroxycarbamide) in high-risk patients.

A.html: BCR-ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukaemia, which presents with marked leucocytosis and a myelocyte peak, not isolated erythrocytosis with low EPO. Its presence would actually exclude polycythaemia vera under WHO criteria.
A.text: BCR-ABL1 defines chronic myeloid leukaemia, which presents with marked leucocytosis and a myelocyte peak, not isolated erythrocytosis with low EPO. Its presence would actually exclude polycythaemia vera under WHO criteria.

B.html: CALR mutations occur in essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis but essentially never in polycythaemia vera. They would not explain this erythrocytosis with suppressed erythropoietin and aquagenic pruritus.
B.text: CALR mutations occur in essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis but essentially never in polycythaemia vera. They would not explain this erythrocytosis with suppressed erythropoietin and aquagenic pruritus.

C.html: MPL W515L is found in a minority of essential thrombocythaemia and myelofibrosis cases. It is not associated with polycythaemia vera and would not account for the raised haematocrit and low EPO here.

D.html: Correct. JAK2 V617F is present in over 95% of polycythaemia vera and causes erythropoietin-independent erythroid proliferation via constitutive JAK-STAT activation. With raised haematocrit and low EPO, it confirms the diagnosis under WHO/BSH criteria.

q: A 5-year-old boy is brought in acutely unwell 24 hours after eating fava beans. He is jaundiced and passing dark urine. His mother reports a similar episode after an antimalarial. Full blood count: Hb 71 g/L, reticulocytes 9%. Blood film shows bite cells, blister cells and irregularly contracted cells; a supravital stain reveals Heinz bodies. Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase are raised, haptoglobin is undetectable. He is of Mediterranean descent. Which single enzyme deficiency BEST explains this presentation?
explain: This is an acute oxidative haemolytic crisis in G6PD deficiency, triggered by fava beans (favism) and previously by an antimalarial (e.g. primaquine). The film — bite cells, blister cells and Heinz bodies — with a negative direct antiglobulin test (excluding autoimmune haemolysis) and intravascular haemolysis markers is characteristic. It is X-linked, so affects boys, and is common in Mediterranean, African and Middle-Eastern populations. 🧬 Mechanism: G6PD catalyses the first step of the pentose phosphate pathway, generating NADPH, which maintains reduced glutathione. Without adequate NADPH, red cells cannot neutralise oxidative stress; haemoglobin oxidises and precipitates as Heinz bodies, which splenic macrophages remove, producing bite cells and haemolysis. Diagnosis is by G6PD enzyme assay (defer until steady state, as reticulocytes have higher enzyme levels and can mask deficiency during a crisis). Management is supportive: remove the trigger, transfuse if severe. Provide a list of drugs/foods to avoid.

A.html: Correct. G6PD deficiency impairs NADPH generation and glutathione recycling, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative stress from fava beans and drugs. Haemoglobin precipitates as Heinz bodies, spleen bites out cells, producing the classic film and DAT-negative haemolysis.

B.html: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes chronic non-spherocytic haemolytic anaemia with echinocytes, but it is not triggered by oxidant exposure and does not produce Heinz bodies or bite cells. The favism trigger points clearly to G6PD deficiency.

C.html: Hexokinase deficiency is a very rare glycolytic enzymopathy causing chronic haemolysis, not episodic oxidative crises with Heinz bodies after fava beans. It does not fit this classic favism presentation.

q: A 24-year-old woman presents with easy bruising and heavy menstrual bleeding. She has a lifelong history of prolonged bleeding after dental extractions and epistaxis. Her mother has similar symptoms. Full blood count is normal including platelets 240 ×10^9/L. Coagulation screen shows a normal prothrombin time and a mildly prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time. Bleeding time is prolonged. Further tests show reduced factor VIII activity, low von Willebrand factor antigen and reduced ristocetin cofactor activity, with normal multimer distribution. Which single mechanism BEST explains the prolonged APTT?
options: Direct inhibition of the intrinsic pathway by an autoantibody
Autosomal recessive deficiency of factor XI
Reduced factor VIII half-life from loss of its carrier protein
Consumption of clotting factors in microvascular thrombi
explain: This is type 1 von Willebrand disease (vWD) — the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, autosomal dominant, causing mucocutaneous bleeding (menorrhagia, epistaxis, bruising, dental bleeding). Investigations show low vWF antigen, reduced ristocetin cofactor activity and normal multimers (quantitative, not qualitative, defect). 🩸 Mechanism of the prolonged APTT: von Willebrand factor is the carrier protein for factor VIII, protecting it from proteolytic degradation in the circulation. When vWF is reduced, factor VIII has a shortened half-life and its plasma level falls. Because factor VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway, its reduction prolongs the APTT while the PT (extrinsic/common pathway) stays normal. The prolonged bleeding time/PFA reflects impaired platelet adhesion, as vWF bridges platelet GPIb to subendothelial collagen. Management (BSH): desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1 releases stored vWF/VIII; tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding; vWF-containing concentrate for major bleeding or surgery.

When vWF is reduced, factor VIII has a shortened half-life and its plasma level falls. Because factor VIII is part of the intrinsic pathway, its reduction prolongs the APTT while the PT (extrinsic/common pathway) stays normal. The prolonged bleeding time/PFA reflects impaired platelet adhesion, as vWF bridges platelet GPIb to subendothelial collagen. Management (BSH): desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1 releases stored vWF/VIII; tranexamic acid for mucosal bleeding; vWF-containing concentrate for major bleeding or surgery.

A.html: An acquired factor inhibitor (e.g. acquired haemophilia) would cause an isolated prolonged APTT that fails to correct on mixing, but it presents with new-onset bleeding in older adults, not a lifelong, familial mucocutaneous pattern with low vWF.

B.html: Factor XI deficiency prolongs the APTT and causes bleeding, but the low vWF antigen, reduced ristocetin cofactor activity and reduced factor VIII here define von Willebrand disease, not a primary factor XI defect.

C.html: Correct. vWF is the plasma carrier for factor VIII; low vWF shortens factor VIII half-life, lowering its level. Reduced factor VIII, an intrinsic-pathway factor, prolongs the APTT while the PT remains normal.

D.html: Consumption of factors in microvascular thrombi describes disseminated intravascular coagulation, which prolongs both PT and APTT with thrombocytopenia and raised D-dimer. This lifelong familial bleeding with normal platelets and PT is not DIC.

E.html: Vitamin K deficiency reduces factors II, VII, IX and X, prolonging the PT first (short-half-life factor VII), then the APTT. Here the PT is normal and vWF is low, which is inconsistent with a vitamin K-dependent factor deficiency.

q: A 29-year-old woman is admitted with confusion, fever and reduced urine output. She had a viral illness a week earlier. Examination shows scattered petechiae and mild jaundice. Full blood count: Hb 79 g/L, platelets 18 ×10^9/L, WCC 9 ×10^9/L. Blood film shows numerous red cell fragments (schistocytes) and reduced platelets. Lactate dehydrogenase is markedly raised, bilirubin elevated, haptoglobin undetectable; direct antiglobulin test is negative. Prothrombin time and APTT are normal. Creatinine is mildly raised. Which single investigation result would MOST specifically confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explain: This is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) — a microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (MAHA) with schistocytes, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, fever and renal involvement (the classic pentad), with a normal coagulation screen distinguishing it from DIC. 🧠 Mechanism: TTP results from severe deficiency of ADAMTS13, the metalloprotease that cleaves ultra-large von Willebrand factor multimers. In acquired TTP an autoantibody inhibits ADAMTS13; the uncleaved ultra-large multimers cause spontaneous platelet aggregation and microvascular thrombi, consuming platelets and shredding red cells (schistocytes). ADAMTS13 activity <10% is diagnostic and the most specific test. Management is a haematological emergency: urgent plasma exchange (do not wait for the assay), plus corticosteroids, rituximab and caplacizumab per BSH guidance. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless life-threatening haemorrhage, as it can fuel thrombosis. Untreated TTP has ~90% mortality; plasma exchange reduces this dramatically.

In acquired TTP an autoantibody inhibits ADAMTS13; the uncleaved ultra-large multimers cause spontaneous platelet aggregation and microvascular thrombi, consuming platelets and shredding red cells (schistocytes). A.html: Raised D-dimer with low fibrinogen indicates disseminated intravascular coagulation, but the PT and APTT here are normal, excluding DIC. TTP characteristically has a normal coagulation screen despite the microangiopathic haemolysis.

B.html: Shiga toxin points to typical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, which predominantly affects children with bloody diarrhoea and prominent acute kidney injury. This adult with a neurological-predominant pentad and only mild renal impairment fits TTP, confirmed by ADAMTS13.

C.html: A positive DAT would indicate autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, but the DAT here is negative and the film shows schistocytes, indicating a mechanical microangiopathic process. AIHA does not produce fragmentation or severe thrombocytopenia with normal clotting.
C.text: A positive DAT would indicate autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, but the DAT here is negative and the film shows schistocytes, indicating a mechanical microangiopathic process. AIHA does not produce fragmentation or severe thrombocytopenia with normal clotting.

D.html: Correct. Severely reduced ADAMTS13 activity (<10%) is specific for TTP. Loss of this vWF-cleaving protease leaves ultra-large multimers that drive platelet-rich microthrombi, producing the schistocytes, thrombocytopenia and organ ischaemia seen here.

q: A 72-year-old man is found to have a raised white cell count on routine testing. He has no symptoms and no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly. Full blood count: Hb 138 g/L, platelets 190 ×10^9/L, WCC 42 ×10^9/L with a lymphocytosis of 36 ×10^9/L. Blood film shows numerous small mature lymphocytes and characteristic smudge (smear) cells. Immunophenotyping shows CD5-positive, CD23-positive, CD19-positive B cells with weak surface immunoglobulin. There is no anaemia or thrombocytopenia. Which single statement about his prognosis or staging is MOST accurate?
options: He is Binet stage A and can be managed with watchful waiting
Immediate chemoimmunotherapy improves survival at this stage
The smudge cells indicate imminent Richter transformation
A 17p deletion would predict an excellent response to fludarabine
Presence of the Philadelphia chromosome confirms the diagnosis
explain: This is chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL): a mature B-cell lymphocytosis with smudge cells and the hallmark immunophenotype CD5+, CD19+, CD23+ with weak surface immunoglobulin. 🩸 Staging: he has lymphocytosis only, with normal Hb, platelets and no organomegaly/lymphadenopathy — this is Binet stage A (fewer than three involved lymphoid areas, no cytopenias). The evidence-based standard (BSH/ESMO) for early-stage, asymptomatic CLL is watchful waiting; multiple trials show no survival benefit from early treatment. Treatment is indicated only for progressive/symptomatic disease (bulky or symptomatic nodes, marrow failure with anaemia/thrombocytopenia, rapid lymphocyte doubling, or systemic symptoms). Adverse markers include del(17p)/TP53 mutation (predicts poor response to chemoimmunotherapy — use BTK inhibitors or venetoclax instead) and unmutated IGHV. Smudge cells are simply fragile lymphocytes, not a marker of Richter transformation (transformation to aggressive lymphoma). BCR-ABL/Philadelphia defines CML, not CLL.

B.html: Randomised trials consistently show no survival benefit from treating asymptomatic early-stage CLL. Immediate chemoimmunotherapy exposes the patient to toxicity without prolonging life, so it is not recommended at Binet stage A.

C.html: Smudge cells are fragile lymphocytes ruptured during smear preparation and are simply a feature of CLL. They do not indicate Richter transformation, which presents with rapidly enlarging nodes, systemic symptoms and rising LDH.

q: A 26-year-old man presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy for 2 months, drenching night sweats, weight loss and intermittent fever. He reports pain in an enlarged node after drinking alcohol. Examination confirms rubbery cervical and mediastinal lymphadenopathy on imaging. Excision lymph node biopsy shows large binucleate cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli in a mixed inflammatory background; these cells are CD15-positive and CD30-positive. Full blood count is normal; lactate dehydrogenase and ESR are raised. Which single finding is MOST characteristic of the underlying diagnosis?
options: Reed–Sternberg cells that are CD15 and CD30 positive
Starry-sky appearance with a very high proliferation index
CD5 and CD23 positive small B lymphocytes
explain: This is classical Hodgkin lymphoma: a young adult with painless cervical/mediastinal lymphadenopathy, B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fever), the characteristic alcohol-induced nodal pain, and a biopsy showing Reed–Sternberg cells — large binucleate ('owl-eye') cells that are CD15+ and CD30+ — in a reactive inflammatory background. 🎗️ Mechanism: Reed–Sternberg cells are the malignant clone (germinal-centre B-cell origin) but form a minority of the tumour; they secrete cytokines recruiting eosinophils, lymphocytes and plasma cells, producing the mixed cellularity and constitutional symptoms. Contrast with non-Hodgkin lymphomas: t(14;18)/BCL2 is follicular lymphoma; 'starry-sky' with a near-100% Ki-67 is Burkitt lymphoma; IgM paraprotein with hyperviscosity is Waldenström macroglobulinaemia; CD5+/CD23+ small B cells indicate CLL/SLL. Staging is by Ann Arbor (with A/B for symptoms); PET-CT guides response-adapted ABVD chemotherapy ± radiotherapy, with high cure rates.

Staging is by Ann Arbor (with A/B for symptoms); PET-CT guides response-adapted ABVD chemotherapy ± radiotherapy, with high cure rates.

A.html: The t(14;18) translocation driving BCL2 overexpression is the hallmark of follicular lymphoma, a non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma. It does not characterise Hodgkin lymphoma, whose diagnostic cell is the CD15/CD30-positive Reed–Sternberg cell.

C.html: A starry-sky appearance with a near-100% proliferation index characterises Burkitt lymphoma, a highly aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphoma with MYC translocation. It does not describe the mixed-cellularity, Reed–Sternberg-containing picture of Hodgkin lymphoma.

q: A 55-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer becomes acutely unwell with widespread bruising, bleeding from venepuncture sites and haematuria. Blood pressure is 90/55 mmHg. Full blood count: Hb 78 g/L, platelets 42 ×10^9/L, WCC 12 ×10^9/L. Blood film shows red cell fragments and reduced platelets. Coagulation screen: prothrombin time prolonged, APTT prolonged, fibrinogen low at 0.7 g/L (1.5–4.0), D-dimer markedly raised. She has been anuric for several hours. Which single management step is the MOST appropriate priority alongside treating the underlying malignancy?
options: Prothrombin complex concentrate to correct the PT
Supportive blood component replacement guided by results and bleeding
Tranexamic acid as sole haemostatic therapy
Platelet transfusion only when count falls below 10 ×10^9/L
explain: This is acute, bleeding-predominant disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) triggered by malignancy: prolonged PT and APTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, thrombocytopenia and schistocytes reflect consumption of platelets and clotting factors with secondary fibrinolysis. 🩸 Mechanism: widespread tissue-factor exposure drives systemic thrombin generation, consuming fibrinogen, platelets and factors, producing simultaneous microvascular thrombosis (organ failure, anuria) and haemorrhage. Management (BSH DIC guideline): the cornerstone is treating the underlying cause, plus supportive replacement of blood components in the actively bleeding patient guided by lab results — fresh frozen plasma for prolonged PT/APTT, cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen concentrate if fibrinogen <1.5 g/L (especially with bleeding), and platelets for significant thrombocytopenia with bleeding (typically keep >50 ×10^9/L in active bleeding). Do not transfuse solely to correct numbers in a non-bleeding patient. Heparin is reserved for thrombosis-dominant DIC without bleeding; PCC is not recommended (it lacks all consumed factors and can aggravate DIC); tranexamic acid alone is generally avoided as it can worsen thrombosis.
